title: Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome and Bone Stress Injuries

blocks.text: **Medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS, "shin splints")** is exercise-related pain along the inner border of the tibia over at least 5 cm, common in runners and military recruits [Ref – to verify]. **Bone stress injuries** range from bone stress reaction to complete stress fracture, caused by repeated loading faster than bone can adapt. Risk factors include rapid training increase, low energy availability (Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport, RED-S), menstrual disturbance, low vitamin D, previous stress fracture and low bone density [Ref – to verify].

Some sites are **high risk** for poor healing or complete fracture: femoral neck (tension side), anterior tibial cortex, navicular, fifth metatarsal base, medial malleolus, sesamoids [Ref – to verify].

sections.title: D to E. Examination and tests

rows: Run fingers along the medial tibia
Diffuse tenderness over 5 cm: MTSS; focal point: stress fracture
Hop 10 times on the affected leg
Focal pain: possible bone stress injury
Place a vibrating fork on the painful bone
Pain may suggest fracture; accuracy limited [Ref – to verify]
Calf and foot strength (heel raise capacity)

blocks.text: Imaging (MRI) is used to confirm and grade bone stress injury when suspected, especially at high-risk sites.
Stress fracture, compartment syndrome, popliteal artery entrapment (claudication, pulse changes), tibial tumour (night pain), radiculopathy.

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Focal tibial pain worsening with walking, night pain
Anterior tibial "dreaded black line" on X-ray, high-risk site
Groin pain with hopping in a runner
Severe leg pain after trauma, pain on passive stretch, tense compartment
Missed periods, low weight, repeated fractures

steps: **Focal tenderness, positive hop test, or high-risk site?** Treat as bone stress injury; reduce load; imaging.
**Diffuse medial tibial tenderness, no focal signs:** working diagnosis MTSS.
**Screen energy availability and bone health in all bone stress injuries.**

items: **Load management (core)**: reduce running to a pain-free level; replace with cycling, swimming or deep-water running.

**Graded return to running** (example): walk-run intervals on alternate days once walking and hopping are pain-free; increase total volume gradually and avoid large week-to-week jumps [Ref – to verify].
**Strength**: calf raises (bent and straight knee), tibialis posterior, hip and knee strengthening, plyometrics before return to sport.
**Running technique**: a modest increase in cadence may reduce loading per step [Ref – to verify]. **Bone health**: adequate energy intake, calcium and vitamin D via medical and dietitian advice.
**Manual therapy and modalities**: minor role. Shockwave: limited evidence [Ref – to verify].

blocks.text: Pain-free hop count, palpation tenderness, run time without pain, heel raise capacity.

items: **How do you separate MTSS from stress fracture on palpation?** Diffuse tenderness over a long segment versus focal point tenderness.
**What is RED-S?** Low energy availability affecting body systems including bone health and menstrual function.
**Name three high-risk stress fracture sites.** Femoral neck (tension side), anterior tibia, navicular.
**Why replace running with cross-training?** To maintain fitness while bone adapts.
**Pain building at the same distance each run with foot numbness that settles on stopping?** Chronic exertional compartment syndrome.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Distinguish MTSS, stress fracture and compartment syndrome.
Plan a graded return to running.
